analysis.one_liner: Taxes private equity and hedge fund managers' profit share as ordinary income rather than at the lower capital gains rate.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 15 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate funds are typically paid a share of the fund's profits, called carried interest, which under current law is taxed at the long-term capital gains rate (20% for top earners) instead of the top ordinary income rate (37%). This bill would tax that profit share as ordinary income, subject it to self-employment taxes, and impose a 40% penalty on underpayments that avoid the rule. Managers who invest their own actual capital would still pay capital gains rates on those returns, and family partnerships are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers broadly, because a small group of very high earners would pay the same rates on their pay that salaried workers pay on wages, and the federal government would collect additional revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Treats the profit share earned by investment managers as ordinary income, taxed at ordinary rates up to 37% instead of the 20% top capital gains rate [S2][S3].
Subjects carried interest income to self-employment taxes, the way wages and professional fees are treated [S2][S3].
Imposes a doubled 40% penalty (instead of the standard 20%) on underpayments that result from misclassifying carried interest [S2][S3].

Protects genuine capital: returns on a manager's own invested money (a qualified capital interest) keep capital gains treatment, so the bill targets compensation for services, not investment returns [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate investment fund managers, whose compensation would be taxed at ordinary income rates plus self-employment tax, and whose industry argues the change would discourage risk-taking and push deals and funds overseas.

drawbacks.text: The industry's core argument is that a manager's profit share is partly a return on risk and effort building companies over years, not a fee for services, so ordinary-income treatment mislabels it and could reduce investment in startups and buyouts. The bill rejects this by keeping capital gains rates for managers' own invested money, but the judgment that carried interest is fundamentally compensation is a policy choice, not a settled fact [S2][S3].

The bill carves out family investment partnerships and includes a 10-year transition for publicly traded partnerships, so some carried interest would have kept its current treatment for a decade or indefinitely [S2][S3].
Real estate held for rental or investment is covered, but partnerships owned by real estate investment trusts get exceptions, leaving room for restructuring to avoid the tax [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls almost entirely on a small group of very high earners, who would pay roughly the same rate on their pay that professionals pay on their income, while genuine capital gains keep their lower rate. The main honest objections are that the industry would pass some costs through fund structures and that the exceptions (family partnerships, REIT-owned partnerships, the public partnership transition) complicate the rules. On the merits the bill's benefits are broad but diffuse and its costs concentrated, which is exactly the pattern that makes it hard to pass.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bill Pascrell introduced the bill on February 15, 2021, with five original cosponsors (Andy Levin, Katie Porter, Don Beyer, Tom Suozzi, Earl Blumenauer), and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means that day [S1][S3][S5].
Fifteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total; no Republican signed on [S4].

The Ways and Means Committee took no further action on the bill; the complete action history ends with the referral, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden had introduced a parallel carried interest bill and included it in Democrats' 2022 tax package, but the provision was dropped from the final Inflation Reduction Act after Sen. Kyrsten Sinema objected, and the House bill never became part of that negotiation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate fund managers, who keep paying the 20% capital gains rate on compensation that would have been taxed at up to 37% plus self-employment tax, with no penalty for misclassification.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers keeping their tax break

for.name: Bill Pascrell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the original cosponsors.

for.name: 15 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the five original cosponsors (Levin, Porter, Beyer, Suozzi, Blumenauer).

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup; the action history ends with the referral.

against.name: Kyrsten Sinema
against.what_they_did: Opposed including carried interest tax increases in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, and the provision was dropped, removing carried interest reform from that year's must-pass tax bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors and the sponsor were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote where a partisan split could be measured.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Their profit-based compensation would be taxed at up to 37% plus self-employment tax instead of 20%, and misclassifying it would carry a 40% penalty. Their pay is among the highest in the economy, so the change raises revenue from a very small, very wealthy group.

Carried interest on startup and fund investments is a specified asset class under the bill, so VC partners' profit shares would be treated as ordinary income; the industry argues this would shrink investment in young companies.

Real estate held for rental or investment is covered, but partnerships owned by publicly traded REITs and genuine capital contributions get exceptions, so some real estate carry would keep its current treatment.

industries.industry: Ordinary investors who contribute actual capital
industries.note: Returns on a manager's own invested money (a qualified capital interest) keep capital gains treatment, preserving the lower rate for genuine investment rather than closing it for everyone.
